Violences conjugales dans les relations: Intimate Partner Violence in Lesbian Relationships: The Long Road for Victims
Les victimes de violence conjugale dans: Victims of intimate partner violence in couples of women suffer from a lack of representation and resources.
Dans mon premier article pour La Convers: In my first article for La Converse, I looked at intimate partner violence in couples of women. Even as media coverage of femicide and heterosexual intimate partner violence grows, LGBTQ+ communities remain absent from the conversation.
Pourtant, ce type de violence existe aus: Yet this type of violence exists in lesbian couples too. As in the rest of society, power dynamics can take hold and lead to psychological or physical violence. Some forms of violence are also specific to the context of sexual and gender minorities.
Le tabou entourant les violences conjuga: The taboo surrounding violence in lesbian relationships makes it harder for victims to recognize what is happening, to access support and to rebuild their lives. They often face a double burden: being victims and belonging to a marginalized community.
Pour comprendre leur réalité et leurs be: To understand their reality and their needs, I spoke with three women who experienced violence at the hands of an ex-partner. Finding people willing to speak publicly wasn’t easy. Organizations that help victims of intimate partner violence are bound by confidentiality and couldn’t put me in touch with any service users who were interested.
C’est finalement grâce à un groupe Faceb: In the end, it was through a Facebook group that I was able to reach these three women. They still wanted as much confidentiality and distance as possible in our exchanges, which is why they preferred a phone call.
Malgré leurs hésitations initiales, Hélè: Despite their initial hesitation, Hélène, Florence and Olivia* were happy to help make intimate partner violence in lesbian couples more visible. All three hope this article will help other victims recognize themselves in these stories.
<strong>Les victimes de violence conjuga: Victims of intimate partner violence in couples of women suffer from a lack of representation and resources that holds back their awareness and their recovery. We spoke with three women who experienced violence at the hands of their partners.
Alors qu’elle vient à peine de répondre: She has barely answered our call when Hélène* stresses the importance of this article. “I think we don’t talk about it enough,” she says of intimate partner violence in lesbian couples. We ourselves had a great deal of difficulty finding information on the subject.
En théorie, tous les organismes québécoi: In theory, all Quebec organizations that specialize in intimate partner violence are open to victims from LGBTQ+ communities. But according to Audrey Mantha, director of the Centre de solidarité lesbienne (CSL), most of these services “are still heteronormative” and take for granted that intimate partner violence means violence by a man against a woman. “Violence between women is still, unfortunately, downplayed,” she adds, and workers sometimes question victims’ experiences. Working with sexual and gender minorities also requires using appropriate vocabulary, avoiding intrusive questions and taking an intersectional approach, which mainstream organizations are sometimes slow to adopt. As a result, lesbian victims often don’t disclose their partner’s gender when they use these services, or don’t turn to them at all, for fear of facing discrimination, M<sup>s</sup>. Mantha says.
Selon Audrey Mantha, la violence conjuga: According to Audrey Mantha, intimate partner violence can be “physical and sexual, but also psychological and economic.” In lesbian relationships, the violence is mainly psychological, according to sexology researcher Macha Loniewski. She explains this in part by gendered socialization, which teaches women to be more physically reserved. Violence then takes a “more roundabout and emotional” form.
Nous nous sommes entretenus avec Florenc: We spoke with Florence*, who wanted to tell her story to show that violence can also be psychological, “contrary to what people think,” she says. Florence, in her forties, is a teacher outside the city. During her lunch break, while her classroom is empty, she takes the time to call us to talk about the psychological violence she experienced during an 11-year relationship with her ex-wife. Her breath catching at times, she lists the “very subtle” remarks and behaviours she endured every day. “She was constantly making demeaning comments,” “going through my phone,” “gaslit me” and “isolating me from a lot of people,” she recalls. Looking back, she believes that “in lesbian couples, the violence is somehow sneakier.”
Bien que la violence psychologique puiss: Although psychological violence can be similar to what is experienced in heterosexual couples, some of its forms are specific to the LGBTQ+ context. Because her partner wasn’t out, Florence was expected to be “discreet” about her sexual orientation. “I used to dress in a more masculine way, I had short hair, but then I just didn’t feel like it anymore” because of the pressure from her partner. According to Audrey Mantha, identity-based belittling is one of the “specific forms” of lesbian intimate violence. It involves devaluing or humiliating one’s partner because of her LGBTQ+ identity. Forced outing, which means revealing a partner’s identity or orientation without her consent, is also a form specific to queer violence.
Malgré la gravité des violences psycholo: Despite how serious psychological violence is, victims don’t always grasp the extent of the situation. “I didn’t see anything for 11 whole years!” Florence says with regret. “Naming the violence is hard because we always imagine it has to be something huge. […] I was never pushed or hit; maybe it would have been more obvious to realize it if I had been,” she concedes. The idea that violence is first and foremost physical remains deeply rooted in victims’ minds, leading them to downplay harmful psychological behaviours in spite of themselves. “It’s little things, really ordinary, everyday things. Taken one by one, they seem insignificant,” Florence says.
La difficulté qu’ont les victimes lesbie: Lesbian victims’ difficulty in understanding that they are experiencing violence can be attributed to the abuser’s gender. According to Claudine Thibaudeau, a social worker at SOS violence conjugale, “intimate partner violence is more associated with men,” including in victims’ own minds, which makes it “harder to name when it comes from a woman.” Hélène believes it would indeed have been easier to call the situation violent if the perpetrator had been a man. She explains this by the fact that LGBTQ+ intimate partner violence is “a lot less represented than heterosexual violence.”
C’était le cas d’Olivia*, une résidente: That was the case for Olivia*, a 23-year-old Longueuil resident. After some hesitation, she looks back on her first romantic relationship, which she had as a teenager. Her partner pressured her to have sex, until she forced her to, despite Olivia’s refusal. It was only after “a year or two” that Olivia was able to put the word “rape” on what happened. “I was already fighting for women’s rights, I was outraged by the sexual assaults women could experience. But in my mind, it was impossible that it could happen to me.” Olivia didn’t associate sexual violence with lesbian relationships. “I heard a lot of stories about rapes by extremely violent men, and I didn’t immediately connect them to what I had been through,” she recalls.
« Tout comme dans la société en général,: “Just like in society in general, there are power dynamics within our [LGBTQ+] communities,” Audrey Mantha says. Even if couples of women escape the gender domination of a man over a woman, other mechanisms of domination can take hold. At the Centre de solidarité lesbienne, M<sup>s</sup>. Mantha therefore has to deal with intimate partner violence based on the victim’s gender identity or sexual orientation. Bisexual people, for example, are at greater risk of violence because of myths that they “sleep with everyone or are at high risk of STBBIs,” according to M<sup>s</sup>. Mantha. She also regularly sees discrimination based on a victim’s immigration status. “People without status are really vulnerable when it comes to intimate and partner violence,” M<sup>s</sup>. Mantha says, since their situation can be used as a tool for blackmail by their partner.
Dans la relation violente qu’elle a vécu: In the abusive relationship she lived through, Hélène believes an imbalance had set in along economic and educational lines. “She worked in a field that paid her a lot, and I had a low-paying job, so she was the one bringing in the money.” Her partner took advantage of that financial edge to control her and blackmail her. “She also played on her intellectual superiority,” Hélène says, explaining that her ex-partner sometimes put her down in public because of her lower level of education. “She was good at drawing, math, writing, languages… me, I was the good-for-nothing.”
Pour sa part, Olivia raconte que son ex-: Olivia, for her part, says her ex-girlfriend used her lack of sexual experience to impose her own practices. “She kept telling me she’d already had a relationship, […] and that I wasn’t going to be the one to teach her how to make love, since I had no experience in that.”
Pour Audrey Mantha, être dans une premiè: For Audrey Mantha, being in a first relationship is a vulnerability factor for violence. In a context where LGBTQ+ romantic and sexual representations are rarer, the more inexperienced person knows less about how a relationship works. “You don’t necessarily have the information, and you end up doing things that don’t match what you want, because your partner tells you that’s what a lesbian relationship is.”
« C’est toujours difficile de sortir d’u: “It’s always hard to leave an abusive relationship; it’s rare that it happens all at once,” Audrey Mantha explains. In couples of women, certain dynamics can delay the breakup. Partners share, for example, common oppressions tied to belonging to sexual and gender minorities, which creates a solidarity that makes separation more complicated. “There’s often a greater emotional closeness. So we see victims who want to protect their partner,” explains the CSL director.
C’est une des raisons pour lesquelles Hé: That is one of the reasons Hélène didn’t leave her partner as quickly as she would have liked. “I wanted to help her with that, I wanted to be the saviour, because I think everyone has some good in them. She was such an intelligent person, with a big heart,” she confides. Despite her intention to change her partner’s behaviour, the episodes of violence continued. “Looking back, I should have gotten out much sooner, I shouldn’t have waited eight years.”
Une fois la relation terminée, les viole: Once the relationship is over, the intimate partner violence continues to haunt victims. The consequences are many, starting with those that weigh on LGBTQ+ identity. “Of course, in our communities, there’s going to be a lot of questioning of sexual orientation,” Audrey Mantha says. “It may seem strange,” but she says we have to remember the sometimes difficult journey it takes to live openly in a relationship with a woman. Experiencing violence within such a relationship “is a bit like shattering their ideal.”
De fait, Florence estime que son identit: Indeed, Florence believes her lesbian identity was affected by the violence inflicted by her ex-partner. “I no longer knew who I was allowed to be, even though I’m fully out in general.”
La sexualité peut aussi être touchée, et: Sexuality can also be affected, regardless of the nature of the violence. According to sexology researcher Macha Loniewski, there can be “repercussions on the ability to let go, to be sexually satisfied, […] or to assert consent.” Following her relationship with a sexually violent partner, Olivia has had difficulty communicating with her partners: “I don’t feel free to say when it hurts, when I don’t want to anymore.” The young woman sometimes has to find non-verbal strategies to signal a refusal, out of fear of saying it out loud.
Lors des entretiens que nous avons eus a: In our interviews, the women spoke at length about their relationships and the violence they endured. To the question “What do you need now?”, one answer kept coming back: to talk. After long years of suffering taboo intimate partner violence, victims feel the urge to talk about what happened to them. Despite the embarrassment and fear, Olivia has told those around her, wanting “people to know what had happened.” Florence “needed to talk about it a huge amount afterward, to get [herself] recognized.” Opening up to loved ones was a way of rediscovering her personality and asserting her “right to exist,” when she had felt like “nobody next to her.” As for Hélène, talking with her “two wonderful sisters and her best friend” is an essential source of support.
Tout n’est pas encore réglé, confie-t-el: Not everything is settled yet, she confides: “I want to get my freedom back and be happy, but I’m still stained by this feeling of fear and anger. Because for all those years, I wasn’t able to listen to myself.” She wishes “nothing but the best [for her ex-partner], that she gets better and takes charge of her life.” To victims, she has this to say: “You have every right to be happy, whoever you are. Everyone deserves to have love.”

Violences conjugales chez les lesbiennes: Intimate Partner Violence Among Lesbians: A Long Road to Recognition for Victims
Les victimes de violence conjugale dans: Victims of intimate partner violence in lesbian couples face a glaring lack of recognition, resources and tailored support.
Cette Montréalaise d’une trentaine d’ann: This Montrealer in her thirties is one of three people who agreed to speak with us by phone and share their stories. Her voice soft and composed, she speaks clearly, despite the emotions underlying her account. Her “first serious relationship” lasted eight years. At first, “everything was going well, it was a fairy tale.” But over the years, Hélène came to question her partner’s words and behaviour, which amounted to psychological violence. “The more I got to know her, the more red flags I saw.” Her partner belittled her in public, for example by bringing up her lack of intelligence, cut her off from her loved ones and blackmailed her. She even ended up subjecting her to physical violence. Those assaults marked a turning point and made Hélène realize she was a victim of intimate partner violence.
Le Centre de solidarité lesbienne est au: The Centre de solidarité lesbienne is currently the only organization in Quebec that serves people experiencing domestic and intimate partner violence in lesbian relationships. Based in Montréal, it supports lesbian-queer victims through support groups and individual intervention sessions. It favours a “by and for” approach rooted in the lesbian and queer community. “That’s what makes us strong,” says the director, because victims don’t have to come out to the other service users or to the counsellors. The organization is a gathering place where victims can share their stories collectively. “They need to see that their reality is a shared one,” stresses Ms. Mantha. However, this inclusive support space set up by the CSL remains limited to the few dozen participants the organization can accommodate.
Si peu d’études ont été menées sur la qu: While few studies have been conducted on the issue in Canada, it is estimated that in the United States, 25 to 40% of women in same-sex relationships have experienced intimate partner violence, according to The Williams Institute. Despite this reality, the intimate partner violence discussed in political and media circles remains essentially heterosexual. “The first explanation, I think, is that women live in a society where they’re less visible than men. […] So a couple made up of two women is even less visible,” says Audrey Mantha. As a result, lesbian-queer victims “don’t see themselves in intimate partner violence and don’t have enough information about those kinds of relationships.”
